body:
This may seem odd, but it's not a bug. GDScript doesn't have generic types like `PackedScene[Node2D]`, so `PackedScene.instantiate()` is of type `Node`, not a concrete type like `Node2D`. Autocompletion shouldn't suggest `Node2D` methods in both cases.

The reason this works for local variables is that the GDScript editor tries to execute code for constant expressions when possible. I.e., it **literally** instantiates the scene, since preloaded resources are treated as constant expressions. While this may be convenient, it is dangerous behavior that may have unexpected side effects.

This doesn't work for class members, because their value may change outside of the function call, so the static analyzer and editor rely only on the declared type.

If you want the most accurate completion suggestions, I would recommend specifying the most accurate type when declaring the variable, like this:

```gdscript
var ex: Node2D = EXAMPLE_SCENE.instantiate()
```

Note that there is a bug in the editor that sometimes removes completion despite having a declared type (you can use the `as` operator as a workaround, although it is not entirely correct).

> If you want the most accurate completion suggestions, I would recommend specifying the most accurate type when declaring the variable, like this:
> 
> var ex: Node2D = EXAMPLE_SCENE.instantiate()

Node is the most accurate type in this case, as it is just an example. 

I usually use the exact type for everything, but I encountered this issue when I wanted to instantiate a Scene which didn't have a class_name to begin with, nor really needed one for the foreseeable future; I wanted to avoid having to give it one just for that one situation.
I was pleasantly surprised to find out that I had fully typed suggestions in local scope, and found it odd when I did not get the same in instance scope. 
I guess the actual unexpected behavior is that we get typed suggestion in local scope then, although that's not really undesirable.
